pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** What Living Things Need

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y2 Animals including humans & Y2 Plants):** "find out about and describe the basic needs of animals, including humans, for survival (water, food and air)" and "find out and describe how plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy." The two need-lists are deliberately DIFFERENT and children compare them.

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-LS1-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-LS1-1]." DCI LS1.C: all animals need food and get it from plants or other animals; plants need water and light. The emphasis is on OBSERVING PATTERNS across many organisms, not memorising a list.

- **Operational details:** Teach need as something that has CONSEQUENCES when withheld — the concept only becomes real when the child sees what happens if a need is missing. Run the classic split-plant investigation (one plant with water/light, one deprived) and observe over days; the wilting plant is the evidence that anchors 'need'. For animals, build on the child's own experience (hunger, thirst, needing air) and extend it to other animals. Crucially, contrast the two lists: animals need FOOD (they cannot make their own), plants need LIGHT (they make their own food) — this seeds the later idea that animals depend on plants. Keep 'air' concrete (we breathe; a candle/animal needs air) without going into gas exchange.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can list animal needs (water, food, air, shelter/warmth) and plant needs (water, light, air, suitable temperature) and predict a consequence of a missing need ("no water → the plant wilts"). Appropriate here: observing and describing over days. NOT appropriate: mechanism (photosynthesis, respiration as gas exchange) — that is KS2/KS3. Watch for the over-generalisation that plants 'eat' soil food like animals.
bestPractices: Define 'need' through consequence: run a controlled deprivation (one watered/lit plant vs one deprived) and observe over days so children see that a missing need causes a visible change.
Explicitly contrast the animal list (needs food it cannot make) with the plant list (needs light and makes its own food) to seed the animals-depend-on-plants idea.
Build animal needs from the child's own body experience (hunger, thirst, breathing) then generalise the pattern to other animals, per the NGSS observe-patterns emphasis.
Keep 'air' and 'warmth' concrete and observational; avoid mechanism (photosynthesis, gas exchange) which belongs to later key stages.
Change one variable at a time in any investigation so the cause of a change is unambiguous to young children.
keyRepresentations: Split-plant fair test: identical plants, one given water/light, one deprived, observed over a week.
Two parallel 'need charts' side by side — animal needs vs plant needs — to make the contrast visible.
A care/keep-alive scenario (windowsill or terrarium) where each need is a supply the child provides.
Need → consequence pairing cards ('no water → wilts', 'no food → weak', 'no light → pale').
commonMisconceptions: 'Plants get their food from the soil' — treating soil/water as food and missing that plants make food from light.
Assuming plants and animals need the SAME things (e.g. that plants need to be 'fed' food, or that animals photosynthesise).
Thinking a need is optional or cosmetic rather than survival-critical, because consequences are slow and unseen.
Confusing 'want' with 'need' (a pet 'needs' a toy) — not distinguishing survival needs from comforts.

learn.summary: For 5–7 year olds learning what living things need to survive. The core idea is that a 'need' is defined by what happens when it is withheld: observing a visible consequence (a wilting plant) anchors the concept. Children build animal needs from their own body experience (hunger, thirst, breathing), then compare the animal list (needs food it cannot make) with the plant list (needs light and makes its own food), seeding the later idea that animals depend on plants. Keep air and warmth concrete and observational; avoid mechanism (photosynthesis, gas exchange) which belongs to later key stages.

activities.title: Side-by-side windowsill care bench
feedback: If a learner gives only water and expects the plant to thrive in the dark, point to the pale, leggy growth: water alone is not enough; the plant also needs light.
If a learner tries to give the plant a food bowl, note that a plant in the light grows without one because it makes its own food using light — only the animal needs feeding.
When a learner restores a missing need and the plant recovers, name it: 'You found the need — without light it went pale; back in the light, its new leaves turn green and it grows stronger.'
Reinforce that changing one thing at a time (e.g. only the light) shows clearly what caused the change.
activities.rationale: Defining 'need' through a controlled deprivation is intended to make the abstract concept concrete and survival-critical for young children, and running plant and animal cases in parallel makes the contrast between the two need-lists visible, seeding the animals-depend-on-plants idea. Standards emphasise observing patterns of what organisms need rather than memorising a list.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y2 requires pupils to describe the basic needs of animals, including humans, for survival (water, food and air), and separately that plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy.

NGSS K-LS1-1 asks children to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-LS1-1] need to survive; DCI LS1.C states all animals need food (obtained from plants or other animals) and plants need water and light.
learnerActions: Set up (or run a model of) two living things to care for: a bean plant in a pot and a small animal such as a hamster in a hutch.

Choose what to provide to each from a shared set of supplies: a watering can, a lamp for light, air, warmth, and a food bowl. With a real hamster, always give it everything it needs; only leave needs out in the model.
Give the plant water but leave it in the dark, and watch over time (days, or time-compressed in a model) to see it stay alive but grow pale and leggy.
Notice that the plant has NO food bowl and still grows, while the animal must be fed — then explain why the two lists differ.
Rescue a wilting or pale plant by restoring the one missing need, and describe what changed.
activities.intendedInsight: A need is proven by its consequence: withhold it and the living thing visibly suffers. Plants and animals need different things — plants need light and make their own food, animals cannot make food and must be fed.

activities.title: Classroom split-plant fair test over a week
feedback: A prediction that the dark plant 'will be fine because it has water' reveals the water-is-enough view; use the observed pale, weak growth to show light is also essential.
A prediction that it goes pale and weak 'because it also needs light' shows an understanding of multiple needs — affirm and extend to air and suitable temperature.
Emphasise the fairness of the test: both plants had the same water, soil and temperature, so a clear difference is most likely due to the one thing we changed — light.
activities.rationale: A real, slow investigation lets children witness that a missing need causes a visible change over time, and the one-variable design helps make the cause clear for young learners. The prediction-and-reason step is diagnostic of whether a child holds a single-need or multiple-need view.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-LS1-1 asks children to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-LS1-1] need to survive; DCI LS1.C states all animals need food (obtained from plants or other animals) and plants need water and light.
learnerActions: Plant two identical seedlings and give both equal water.
Place one in a bright spot and cover the other with a lightproof box (or put it in a dark cupboard) in the same room, keeping water, pot, soil and temperature as similar as possible.
Before the week passes, predict whether the dark seedling will grow as healthily (green and sturdy) as the light one, and say WHY. Remember a plant in the dark may grow taller but pale and floppy.
Observe both plants over several days and record what changes.
Compare the result to the prediction and state which need was missing from the weaker plant.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing only one variable (light) while keeping water, temperature and everything else as similar as possible shows that light is a genuine need for healthy growth: water alone is not enough.

activities.title: Name the needs and what uses them
feedback: If a learner names only a healthy state, prompt: 'What if this one were missing — what would you see?'
If a learner lists animal needs for the plant (e.g. a food bowl), revisit that the plant makes its own food from light and does not eat.
Confirm correct need–part pairings and have the learner say the matching consequence.
activities.rationale: Naming the needs cleanly and tying each to a body part or behaviour supports the standards' need-lists; pairing each with its consequence keeps the concept causal rather than a memorised list. This is a naming/recall-supporting activity: a reveal scene can name each need and show a prepared picture of the missing-need state, but it does not let the child dynamically cause and observe the deprivation, so it works best alongside the deprivation investigations that build the causal insight.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y2 requires pupils to describe the basic needs of animals, including humans, for survival (water, food and air), and separately that plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy.
learnerActions: Look at a plant and an animal and name each basic need aloud: for the plant — water, light, air, suitable temperature; for the animal — water, food, air, shelter/warmth.
Pair each need with the part or behaviour that uses it, e.g. roots take up water, leaves use light, the animal's mouth takes in food.
For each need, say what the living thing would look like if that need were missing (e.g. 'no water → wilts', 'no light → pale', 'no food → weak').
activities.intendedInsight: Each need is linked to a part or behaviour of the organism and to a specific consequence if it is missing.

activities.title: Sort and match: plant needs, animal needs, both
feedback: If a learner places a food bowl under 'plant needs', revisit that soil and water are not the plant's food — the plant makes food from light; soil gives water and support.
If a learner says 'plants get their food from the soil', explain that at this age we establish plants need light to grow and make their own food.
Confirm correct sorts by having the learner say which needs are shared and which differ.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and matching check whether a child has internalised the comparison between the two lists, and the chosen common misconception directly surfaces the soil-as-food error. This activity checks recall of the lists rather than building the causal insight on its own, so pair it with the investigations.
sourceClaims: Children commonly hold that plants get their food from the soil like animals eat, rather than making their own food from light — a persistent teleological/animal-analogy misconception to address when contrasting plant and animal needs.
learnerActions: Sort need cards into three groups: 'plant needs', 'animal needs', and 'both'.
Match each 'need' card to a 'consequence of lacking it' card (e.g. no water → wilts; no food → weak; no light → pale).
Consider the common wrong idea that 'plants get their food from the soil' and explain why it is incorrect.
Optionally use a 'how much water' slider to show that too little or too much is a problem.
activities.intendedInsight: The two need-lists overlap (water, air, suitable temperature/warmth) but differ in key ways (plants need light and make their own food; animals need food they cannot make).

activities.title: Talk in-role with a thirsty plant or hungry pet
feedback: If a learner offers a plant food, use the character to redirect: 'I don't eat food — I make mine from light; what I need is...'
Praise correct inferences and ask the learner to name the consequence that would follow if the need stayed unmet.
For the goldfish, confirm that it needs to be in water to breathe and stay alive, so out of water it is missing what it needs; for the worm, confirm that even underground it still needs air.

If a learner says a plant needs to sleep, gently separate the survival needs shared by plants and animals (water, air, suitable conditions — plus light for plants and food for animals) from behaviours like sleeping that not every living thing does.
activities.rationale: In-role dialogue can motivate care-reasoning and elicit children's ideas, which may surface misconceptions. Dialogue describes consequences rather than letting the child observe them, so it complements the deprivation investigations rather than replacing them.
learnerActions: Take part in a conversation where a plant or animal gives graded hints about how it feels (e.g. 'my leaves are drooping...', 'I feel hungry...').
Infer which need is missing from the hints and say what to provide.
Explain, for a plant, why you would NOT offer it food, and for an animal why you would.
Extend the pattern to other animals: say what a goldfish would be missing if it were taken out of the water, and point out that a worm in the soil still needs air.
Talk about whether sleeping is a need that all living things share — note that an animal such as the hamster sleeps but a plant does not, so sleeping is not a universal survival need.
activities.intendedInsight: Caring reasoning — matching a described symptom to the missing need — reinforces that each need has a felt consequence, that the same pattern holds across different animals, and that plant and animal needs differ, with some human/animal behaviours (like sleeping) not being universal needs.

constraints: Keep content at the concrete/observational level for ages 5–7: children list animal needs (water, food, air, shelter/warmth) and plant needs (water, light, air, suitable temperature) and predict a consequence of a missing need.
Do not teach mechanism (photosynthesis, respiration as gas exchange) — that belongs to later key stages. Keep 'air' and 'warmth' concrete (we breathe; a candle or animal needs air).
Address the over-generalisation that plants 'eat' soil food like animals: at this age establish that soil gives water and support, and plants make their own food from light.
Distinguish survival needs from wants/comforts (a pet 'needs' a toy) and from human/animal-specific behaviours (a plant does not need to sleep or have a house).
Change only one variable at a time in any investigation so the cause of a change is unambiguous.
Sort/match and reveal-the-state scenes check recall of the lists; they do not on their own build the causal insight that comes from observing deprivation, so use them alongside an investigation.
A time-compressed care model is a scaffold that compresses the real waiting period; pair it with a real classroom investigation over a week so children see the genuine timescale and evidence.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Legacy source flags: the DfE KS1 claim was marked verified; the NGSS K-LS1-1 claim and the Rueschhoff plant-misconceptions claim were marked not verified. Treat the latter two as unconfirmed.

The legacy row asserted that a live care-sim delivers cause-and-effect 'exactly what a static picture cannot deliver' and that a 3D environment 'adds nothing'. These are catalog-preference claims, not established efficacy findings, and have been removed/softened. A fixed image can still teach the need-lists; a 3D view simply offers a different experience without being necessary or useless for this spatially-independent concept.
The time-compressed model is pedagogically useful but it is a representation, not real growth; retained as a scaffold with the real week-long investigation preserved alongside.

Conceptual audit: a plant watered but kept dark growing pale/leggy while surviving for a while is biologically reasonable for a seedling living on stored reserves; kept qualitative ('pale, weak, eventually dies') rather than asserting an exact timeline.

The DfE wording names plant needs as water, light and a suitable temperature and does not mention air; air is retained as a plant need because it is biologically correct and the original row treats 'plants don't need air' as a misconception to correct. The child-facing plant list therefore includes a need beyond those named in the cited DfE claim.

Concrete probe examples from the source assessment (goldfish out of water, worm in soil, and sleeping as a human/animal-specific behaviour) were restored into the conversation activity and constraints so they are not lost.

assess.poeTask: Grow two identical seedlings with equal water — one on a bright windowsill, one shut in a dark cupboard — for a week. Before the week passes, ask the child to predict whether the dark one will grow as well as the light one, and WHY. The reason is diagnostic: predicting it grows fine 'because it has water' holds the water-is-enough view; predicting it goes pale and weak because it also needs light shows an understanding of multiple needs.
probeDeeper: What would happen to a goldfish if we took it out of the water? Which need is missing?
Does a plant need air? What about a worm in the soil?
A plant needs light, but you need to sleep — is sleeping a need that all living things share?
If we forgot to feed a hamster, which of its needs are we not meeting?
assess.correctAnswer: It won't grow well — it's missing light. Plants need light (as well as water, air and a suitable temperature); without light the plant goes pale, weak and eventually dies, because water alone isn't enough. Living things suffer if any one of their basic needs is missing.

errorPatterns.pattern: plants only really need water (light and air not essential)
errorPatterns.nextMove: list all a plant's needs — water, light, air, suitable temperature — and show light is essential using a dark-grown seedling
errorPatterns.distractor: It will be fine — as long as a plant has water it will grow
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the watered plant will be fine in the dark

errorPatterns.pattern: plants get their food from the soil / plants 'eat' soil
errorPatterns.nextMove: at this age, establish that plants need light to grow and make food; soil gives water and support, it isn't 'food'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the probe says soil is the plant's food and light isn't needed

errorPatterns.pattern: plants don't need air (only animals do)
errorPatterns.nextMove: include air among plant needs, alongside animals'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: omits air from a plant's needs

errorPatterns.pattern: living things need the same things humans do (a plant needs to sleep, or needs a house)
errorPatterns.nextMove: distinguish universal needs (water, air, food/light, suitable conditions) from human-specific wants

responseLevels.gap: Says the plant will be fine with just water, or lists no needs; cannot say what happens when a need is missing.
responseLevels.full: Names the basic needs of both plants (water, light, air, suitable temperature) and animals (water, food, air, shelter), predicts what happens when one is missing, and distinguishes shared needs from human wants.
responseLevels.partial: Lists some needs for plants or animals, but as a memorised list — cannot predict the consequence of a specific missing need, or applies animal needs to plants inconsistently.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A plant is watered every day but kept in a dark cupboard with the door shut. It's getting plenty of water — so will it grow well, or is it missing something it needs? Explain what will happen and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks water is the main thing a plant needs says it'll be fine; a child who knows plants also need light predicts it fails and names the missing need. The reason tier surfaces which needs the child actually holds.
